entry.title: A journey from indoctrination to liberation (Educated by Tara Westover)

link.title: A journey from indoctrination to liberation (Educated by Tara Westover)

entry.content:
“The past is beautiful because one never realises an emotion at the time. It expands later, & thus we don’t have complete emotions about the present, only about the past.” —VIRGINIA WOOLF

“I had been educated in the rhythms of the mountain, rhythms in which change was never fundamental, only cyclical. The same sun appeared each morning, swept over the valley and dropped behind the peak. The snows that fell in winter always melted in the spring. Our lives were a cycle—the cycle of the day, the cycle of the seasons—circles of perpetual change that, when complete, meant nothing had changed at all. I believed my family was a part of this immortal pattern, that we were, in some sense, eternal. But eternity belonged only to the mountain.” —TARA WESTOVER

What if I’m born into a different family? What if I’m born into a different country or century? Would I be the same person?

I asked these question every time I tried to imagine myself in Tara’s life. I was never born into an ultra-religious family, nor was born into one which thinks of the worst possible scenarios all the time. I wasn’t born into a time where I cannot go to the medical establishments when I get sick, nor was born to be indoctrinated rather than educated. I was born into a family, a place and time which I now take for granted.

Unlike me, Tara was born into a family whose beliefs left a deep mark into her life. This mark was destructive, fatalistic, and undeserved. Tara lived a life of danger, made more dangerous by the fact that they did not seek medical help when they truly needed it. Tara was raised to believe that the government is against them, that the medical establishments are there to hurt them—set by the government, and that everyone who aren’t like them are evil-socialist-whore. Tara was not given the opportunity to be educated normally throughout his childhood and adolescence, where she goes to school with people of similar ages because his father believed that schools are brainwashing institution set up by the government. She was born into this world.

But like me, we shared some similarities, or I thought similar enough to feel like we had the same experiences. Those similar experiences echoed throughout the book.

The dangers of false beliefs, either by faith or by fear

I could not help myself but assume that the turning point where Tara’s father became the way he is, fearful and anxious, was when the Ruby Ridge incident happened. The book opened this topic quickly in the beginning and I cannot stop attributing it to his father’s behavior, this is considering how Tara described his father as being a completely different father to his older brothers.

“The older boys—Tony, Shawn and Tyler—had been raised in a different decade, and it was almost as if they’d had different parents. Their father had never heard of the Weavers

That history did something to their father.”

As a result, the rest of their siblings, including Tara, was raised in isolation, no official birth certificates, no attending school, just them at Buck’s Peak. Their father believed that the government is going to target them next, this fear did something to their father. This is a kind of false belief induced by fear.

The other dangerous kind of belief is induced by faith. This kind of faith in something: a God or an idea of something can be seen throughout the book.

Their father believed so much to their faith that he is willingly risking the lives of his children just because he had a false belief against the medical establishments. He thinks that God will cure everything, or he thinks that God has a deterministic plan for their family.

There were many instances in the book where faith won against reason. There were so many things that could have ended badly, or someone could have died. And for what?

A child indoctrinated is a child deprived of freedom

What kind of liberty is lost from indoctrination?

Freedom to think for ourselves, this is what Tara did not have the freedom to do, not until entering college.

The book can be summed up to this phrase: A journey from indoctrination to liberation.

Life in isolation brings a fascinating view into what it means to live a good life

(unfinished)

Truth and change reveals itself slowly, one realization, one shift at a time

(unfinished)

The importance of being educated

(unfinished)

The book ended in a powerful note:

“You could call this selfhood many things. Transformation. Metamorphosis. Falsity. Betrayal.

I call it an education.”
entry.summary: “The past is beautiful because one never realises an emotion at the time. It expands later, & thus we don’t have complete emotions about the present, only about the past.” —VIRGINIA WOOLF

entry.title: Would you feel sympathy for a killer? (Adolescence 2025)

link.title: Would you feel sympathy for a killer? (Adolescence 2025)

entry.content:
Here’s a dilemma: An innocent looking, 13-year-old boy, was accused of killing a girl similar to his age. There was concrete video evidence, but there’s a missing piece—more than the weapon, but the Why?

Motives for crimes are a secondary intel behind the actual evidence—the whys don’t justify the fact. The motive has little or no impact on the verdict to a crime as killing for a reason is not that different to another reason, not unless it is for “self defense” or war, or any other ways we as a society legalized killing another person.

Beyond the dilemma of why, we as the audience, can fall into the trap of the show. They made the accused killer seem innocent, besides, he was just a child—he’s not that scary. We can fall into the trap of attaching hope that this boy will be proven innocent and freed. The show created a facade which can make us sympathize with the accused killer, and I don’t think it’s unreasonable to feel that sympathy especially when watching the first 2 episodes only. The boy pleads he did not do it, and you can see a glimpse in his eyes and tone of voice that he didn’t.

The Season 1 of the show has a limited run of 4 episodes. Episode 1 followed the arrest and initial questioning of the accused. Episode 2 followed the police trying to find answers on the victim and accused killer’s school. Episode 3 followed a psychologist interviewing the boy. And Episode 4 follows the boy’s family months after the chaos.

Episode 1: The chaos

The police raided the Miller family’s house like a terrorist was inside. No showing of search or arrest warrant, just pure force, just to arrest a little boy named Jamie. He was under arrest for suspicion of murder. Obviously, this chaos that ensued brought the boy and his family to feel terror. We followed Jamie on their way to a police facility. What first struck me was how composed he is, he was just 13, the police just arrested him, and he is made to do things that a child must not experience. I won’t spoil much, but I admire how the legal side of this show was at least ethical. I would have hated it if there’s some legal manipulation happening, but even the arresting officers gave respect to the rights of Jamie and his family too. They showed the video evidence in this episode—it showed Jamie following the victim and ultimately stabbing her—he was, as it stands, guilty. But there’s a feeling of not really. Even without the hints of other possibilities, this video still did not convince me that he did it. Jamie’s father, however, did as many viewers are too. But throughout this show, there is a constant choice between seeing Jamie as pure guilty thus evil and seeing and sympathizing with the idea that he was just another victim in this case or that a mental health problem caused him to do what he did. Nonetheless, basing on the facts, he was guilty right then and there. I personally felt sympathy for him, because I wasn’t convinced yet that he did it for some reason. I also wanted to know the Why before passing any judgement. My brain theorized a scenario that he was just set up or if he in fact did it, there’s some mental health issue at play. I know that sympathizing for a criminal is unethical in all ways, but again, he was still accused and therefore was still innocent to me.

Episode 2: The leads

The police continued finding the Why, they haven’t found the weapon and there is no motive. They went to the school that the victim and Jamie went to. They questioned the school and the students, but were met with various red flags. For one, there was a scene where two boys, which I assume are Jamie’s friends, talking about what happened. They mentioned the knife, which immediately raised a red flag, and a hint that Jamie is not a lone actor. My theory that he was set up came from these two boys. Another red flag was the victim’s best friend. The interview act with her just screams that she knows something or she thinks she knows. Later on, she physically abused one of the boys who is a friend of Jamie—she said that he did it—so once again, a hint that it might not be Jamie alone. That same boy even tried to escape when confronted by the police, he was also arrested after admitting that it was his knife which was used. The police did not question the other boy, which is a bit suspicious to me. Finally, one of the police officer’s sons made some confession which I still don’t fully understand. But that confession made his father think of another angle—Jamie is being bullied. The picture is looking clearer: Jamie, if he did do it, was not alone. There is a possibility of the friends setting him up. I just realized I keep saying “setting him up”, I don’t have a concrete definition to this claim but I mean it in a way that Jamie was either provoked to kill her, his friends changed clothes with him to make it look like it’s him, basically conspiracy stuff. Going back to the point, Jamie was bullied by the victim. I think a quote from the show perfectly summarizes what this particular episode is all about; “What you think is more important than what’s true.” Yes, the video evidence exists, but how do we know if there’s a piece of truth that will explain it even better. I wanted to know the full picture rather than the single evidence that Jamie did it.

Episode 3: A masterpiece, a manipulation, and a man confessing

Episode 3 is one of the most brilliant media I’ve ever watched. It is a masterpiece of storytelling, acting, cinematographhy—and everything about it feels perfect. The actor that played Jamie really did a very good job.

Manipulation is a central theme to this act. It feels like the psychologist is manipulating Jamie, and Jamie also does the same. It felt like a trick sometimes, but I think the whole act was not a trick but indeed a conversation. If there’s someone tricking, it was Jamie as evident to his multiple outbursts when he said something that might prove him guilty. Jamie’s character is just brilliant for his age, and it was evident by his ability to manipulate what he is saying, it reflected in his ability to hide. The last 20 minutes, which is just a rough estimate, is where all of the dots started connecting. Jamie revealed a part of himself he’s been hiding from us—he finally said things that seemed like a confession. Until now, he’s been firm in his stand that he did not do it. But what we heard from him, that he had a knife that night but he did not touch her… that doing so made him better than other men… is a clear admission of the truth. I felt what the psychologist probably felt—I wanted Jamie to be proven good, I wanted him to be free, I wanted him to continue saying that he did not do it—but that didn’t happen.

Episode 4: Goodbye

Our goodbye with Jamie happened at the end of Episode 3. It will be the last time we will ever see him apart from a call he will make in this last episode.

This episode followed the life of Jamie’s family 13 months after the chaos. What really struck me was how normal their lives seemed until they were reminded by the effects of what Jamie did. The first reminder was the vandalism in their van saying “NONSE,” which is an insult apparently that also means pedophile. This started the anger of the father. As they went to a store to buy paint, another reminder appeared. A man approached the father which he recognizes, the man followed him saying that he sympathized and is on Jamie’s side. The father was reminded of what happened, his mind went blank, but when they were about to leave, he saw the kids who vandalised his car. This made his anger into a long outrage which can be felt throughout the act. His wife and daughter stayed silent in his outburst, when suddenly, they received a call from Jamie.

Jamie wanted to let his father know that he is pleading guilty. Silence was heard, then Jamie’s mother and sister spoke. Jamie was not expecting to have his mother and sister on the call, which hurts to think about because it seems like he did not trust them. The call got cut before his father could say the word “don’t”. Emotions started rising, when they got home, it flooded the house. We got to witness a conversation between the parents about Jamie. This conversation seems like a goodbye, an acknowledgement that they need to move on. The father ended the show with such a powerful scene—he went to his son’s room, cried, then tucked a teddy bear as if putting Jamie to sleep.

I was watching that ending at around 2 AM, I was sobbing, I was writing in my diary, I was devastated. I felt no closure from Jamie, I wanted to see him again even if that means seeing him sentenced to prison. I wanted to know what his future will hold despite all that happened.

Conclusion

To answer the headline—Yes, I did sympathize with the accused killer. I grew to like the facade of this innocent boy who hasn’t been proven guilty yet. But honestly, the truth is clear. Jamie killed the girl without any doubt. I think the reason why I still felt sympathy was because I was seeing the hardship that Jamie went through while the death of the girl just merely echoed in the background. The show followed the life of Jamie, so we only got to see his perspective. I believed in his statements that he did not do it, that he did nothing wrong, because the only voice saying otherwise was that video evidence which I still don’t understand why it was not enough evidence in the first place. The show made me want to know why—to know what Jamie thinks rather than the clear truth in front of me. In the end, I got answers to the whys, but I wanted to know what will happen next. The show ended with minimal closure to what happened to Jamie. It ended without looking back at what happened to the girl. But maybe it’s better that we don’t know. We left Jamie finally admitting to his sin, and we can try and think of what happened to him after that—we can try and feel sorry for him—but it doesn’t change the fact that he was guilty. And the real victims here besides the girl and her family, was Jamie’s family—who suffered the pain of losing a child and suffered the guilt that they allowed all of this to happen.
entry.summary: Here’s a dilemma: An innocent looking, 13-year-old boy, was accused of killing a girl similar to his age. There was concrete video evidence, but there’s a missing piece—more than the weapon, but the Why?

entry.title: Appreciation of creative works
entry.content:
Someone out there is reading a book,
Someone out there is reading a paper,
Someone out there is reading a poem,
Someone out there is watching a film,
Someone out there is watching a show,
Someone out there is watching a video,
Someone out there is listening to a music,
Someone out there is listening to a podcast episode,
Someone out there is listening to a speech…

All of them being inspired or touched, feeling joy or sadness, experiencing what is it to be and be in a certain place and time, connecting with characters unknown… Someone out there is forever changed because they saw or heard a work that deeply connected with them.

entry.title: History is an inexorable process which man cannot influence (War and Peace by Leo Tolstoy)

link.title: History is an inexorable process which man cannot influence (War and Peace by Leo Tolstoy)

entry.content:
These are some highlights and notes I had when I read War and Peace.

[X] War and Peace is what the author wished and was able to express in the form in which it is expressed.

[XI] History generalizes a whole series of commands ‘into a single expression of will’; but this is simply an illusion and, therefore, a falsehood.

[XI] When in doubt inaction is far preferable to action. Tolstoy endorses this belief at the end of the novel.

[XV] p. 773. I came to this sudden realization that the goal of having a war, no matter how counterintuitive is to have peace… Chapter 16 of Book 12 is the ultimate/best chapter I think so far because I can see how war became the metaphor for life and peace for death. War wants peace but not the other way around. Having peace don’t have the need for war. This is similar to life and death where life has an end of death but death don’t come to be alive…

[57] In this world one has to be cunning and cruel.

[75] God has nothing to do with it! (Religion, surprisingly, will become a topic across this book, I had this pre-conceived notion that Russians are atheist, maybe they are in some eras, but the epoch in this book certainly consists of religious people, but surprisingly, there also exist people who don’t believe in God, as shown in the quote.)

[80] “The only thing that is hard for me… I will tell you the truth, Andrew… is Father’s way of treating religious subjects. I don’t understand how a man of his immense intellect can fail to see what is as clear as day, and can go so far astray. That is the only thing that makes me unhappy. But even in this I can see lately a shade of improvement. His satire has been less bitter of late, and there was a monk he received and had a long talk with.”

[90] “As far as the service goes he is quite punctilious, your excellency; but his character…” said Timókhin.

“And what about his character?” asked the regimental commander.

“It’s different on different days,” answered the captain. “One day he is sensible, well educated, and good-natured, and the next he’s a wild beast…. In Poland, if you please, he nearly killed a Jew.”

[110] “One step beyond that boundary line which resembles the line dividing the living from the dead lies uncertainty, suffering, and death. And what is there? Who is there?—there beyond that field, that tree, that roof lit up by the sun? No one knows, but one wants to know. You fear and yet long to cross that line, and know that sooner or later it must be crossed and you will have to find out what is there, just as you will inevitably have to learn what lies the other side of death. But you are strong, healthy, cheerful, and excited, and are surrounded by other such excitedly animated and healthy men.”

[114] At that instant the sun began to hide behind the clouds, and other stretchers came into view before Rostóv. And the fear of death and of the stretchers, and love of the sun and of life, all merged into one feeling of sickening agitation.

“O Lord God! Thou who art in that heaven, save, forgive, and protect me!”

[115] Pursued by the French army of a hundred thousand men under the command of Bonaparte, encountering a population that was unfriendly to it, losing confidence in its allies, suffering from shortness of supplies, and compelled to act under conditions of war unlike anything that had been foreseen, the Russian army of thirty-five thousand men commanded by Kutúzov was hurriedly retreating along the Danube, stopping where overtaken by the enemy and fighting rearguard actions only as far as necessary to enable it to retreat without losing its heavy equipment.

[126] “But as you are a philosopher, be a consistent one, look at the other side of the question and you will see that your duty, on the contrary, is to take care of yourself. Leave it to those who are no longer fit for anything else…. You have not been ordered to return and have not been dismissed from here; therefore, you can stay and go with us wherever our ill luck takes us…”

  • The Golden Mean: it is the idea that sometimes, things are better left for more capable individuals to take action, as I remember from PewDiePie’s video. Too much of something is not something we want, even in our actions, there can be extremes which must be avoided if we want to be within that mean.

[131] But a freak of fate made the impossible possible.

[132] They talked of peace but did not believe in its possibility; others talked of a battle but also disbelieved in the nearness of an engagement.

[136] “No, friend,” said a pleasant and, as it seemed to Prince Andrew, a familiar voice, “what I say is that if it were possible to know what is beyond death, none of us would be afraid of it. That’s so, friend.”

Another, a younger voice, interrupted him: “Afraid or not, you can’t escape it anyhow.”

“All the same, one is afraid! Oh, you clever people,” said a third manly voice interrupting them both. “Of course you artillery men are very wise, because you can take everything along with you—vodka and snacks.”

And the owner of the manly voice, evidently an infantry officer, laughed.

“Yes, one is afraid,” continued the first speaker, he of the familiar voice. “One is afraid of the unknown, that’s what it is. Whatever we may say about the soul going to the sky… we know there is no sky but only an atmosphere.”

[146] The moral hesitation which decided the fate of battles was evidently culminating in a panic.

[155] Pierre, on unexpectedly becoming Count Bezúkhov and a rich man, felt himself after his recent loneliness and freedom from cares so beset and preoccupied that only in bed was he able to be by himself. He had to sign papers, to present himself at government offices, the purpose of which was not clear to him, to question his chief steward, to visit his estate near Moscow, and to receive many people who formerly did not even wish to know of his existence but would now have been offended and grieved had he chosen not to see them.

[156] It seemed so natural to Pierre that everyone should like him, and it would have seemed so unnatural had anyone disliked him, that he could not but believe in the sincerity of those around him. Besides, he had no time to ask himself whether these people were sincere or not. He was always busy and always felt in a state of mild and cheerful intoxication. He felt as though he were the center of some important and general movement; that something was constantly expected of him, that if he did not do it he would grieve and disappoint many people, but if he did this and that, all would be well; and he did what was demanded of him, but still that happy result always remained in the future.

[171] “If anyone finds this silence inconvenient, let him talk, but I don’t want to,” he seemed to say. Besides this, in his behavior to women Anatole had a manner which particularly inspires in them curiosity, awe, and even love—a supercilious consciousness of his own superiority. It was as if he said to them: “I know you, I know you, but why should I bother about you? You’d be only too glad, of course.”

[181] The universal experience of ages, showing that children do grow imperceptibly from the cradle to manhood, did not exist for the countess. Her son’s growth toward manhood, at each of its stages, had seemed as extraordinary to her as if there had never existed the millions of human beings who grew up in the same way. As twenty years before, it seemed impossible that the little creature who lived somewhere under her heart would ever cry, suck her breast, and begin to speak, so now she could not believe that that little creature could be this strong, brave man, this model son and officer that, judging by this letter, he now was.

[186] It is very difficult to tell the truth, and young people are rarely capable of it.

[199] “All eventualities have been foreseen…”

[203]

  • In waging war, it is often better not to attack if there is no gain foreseen, but one must be ready to defend or wage attack in an instant if enemy movements shows an increasing possibility of an attack. Waiting often signals to the enemy that you are not capable of attacking so the importance of being selective on waging but still being ready is utmost in winning.

[217] All is vanity, all falsehood, except that infinite sky. There is nothing, nothing, but that. But even it does not exist, there is nothing but quiet and peace.

[226] “The praise of a great commander is a soldier’s highest reward,” said Repnín.

[227] How good it would be to know where to seek for help in this life, and what to expect after it beyond the grave! How happy and calm I should be if I could now say: ‘Lord, have mercy on me!’… But to whom should I say that? Either to a Power indefinable, incomprehensible, which I not only cannot address but which I cannot even express in words—the Great All or Nothing-” said he to himself, “or to that God who has been sewn into this amulet by Mary! There is nothing certain, nothing at all except the unimportance of everything I understand, and the greatness of something incomprehensible but all-important.

[234] He was at the period of youth when there seems so much to do that there is no time for that sort of thing and a young man fears to bind himself and prizes his freedom which he needs for so many other things.

[246 ] Pierre was one of those people who, in spite of an appearance of what is called weak character, do not seek a confidant in their troubles. He digested his sufferings alone.

[246] “Louis XVI was executed because they said he was dishonorable and a criminal,” came into Pierre’s head, “and from their point of view they were right, as were those too who canonized him and died a martyr’s death for his sake. Then Robespierre was beheaded for being a despot. Who is right and who is wrong? No one! But if you are alive—live: tomorrow you’ll die as I might have died an hour ago. And is it worth tormenting oneself, when one has only a moment of life in comparison with eternity?”

[247] “So it seems you’re a hero, eh? Come now, what was this duel about? What is it meant to prove? What? I ask you.”

Pierre turned over heavily on the ottoman and opened his mouth, but could not reply.

“If you won’t answer, I’ll tell you…” Hélène went on. “You believe everything you’re told. You were told…” Hélène laughed, “that Dólokhov was my lover,” she said in French with her coarse plainness of speech, uttering the word amant as casually as any other word, “and you believed it! Well, what have you proved? What does this duel prove? That you’re a fool, que vous êtes un sot, but everybody knew that. What will be the result? That I shall be the laughingstock of all Moscow, that everyone will say that you, drunk and not knowing what you were about, challenged a man you are jealous of without cause.” Hélène raised her voice and became more and more excited, “A man who’s a better man than you in every way…”

[253-254]

  • The Death of Princess Mary: I remember 2 or 3 instances in this book were Tolstoy’s writing changed the events dramatically in just a Chapter. This is one of the first. As you are reading the chapter, it starts like all is well: the baby is being born then he makes it seem like all is okay, he hides the fact that a character was gone for a few sentences or so, immersing you with a different perspective without seeing anything bad, then he slaps you with the truth. I was amazed at how he conveys something as extreme as death in the most surprising and unexpected ways possible.

[255] I know people consider me a bad man!” he said. “Let them! I don’t care a straw about anyone but those I love; but those I love, I love so that I would give my life for them, and the others I’d throttle if they stood in my way.

[257] Seize the moments of happiness, love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world, all else is folly.

[257] As soon as he entered he noticed and felt the tension of the amorous air in the house, and also noticed a curious embarrassment among some of those present. Sónya, Dólokhov, and the old countess were especially disturbed, and to a lesser degree Natásha. Nicholas understood that something must have happened between Sónya and Dólokhov before dinner, and with the kindly sensitiveness natural to him was very gentle and wary with them both at dinner. On that same evening there was to be one of the balls that Iogel (the dancing master) gave for his pupils during the holidays.
entry.summary: These are some highlights and notes I had when I read War and Peace.

entry.title: Reading The World-Ending Fire
entry.content:
I attempted to read this book two times before. I discovered it in a Jared Henderson book recommendation video on YouTube some year or two ago. The title hooked me so much that I romanticized reading it, and I even made my first blog referencing the title. But enough of my chatter, I have some words upon finishing this collection of essays by Wendell Berry. This book is long and dense, and requires more reading concentration to get something out of it, so here are some thoughts that remained from my reading.

The most important points to get from reading this is the author’s advocacy for a society that is local rather than global, it ties with his main advocacy of caring for the environment, particularly the lands. As a farmer, and an old man, he definitely experienced living the life he is advocating. His philosophy centers around the careful stewardship of nature, by not letting the future, and its innovations run on his life. His philosophy advocates for the careful consideration that innovation, globalization, industrialization, and any -ions brought about by the future are the reasons for the destruction of nature.

He is akin to Henry David Thoreau in a sense because he is advocating that the way to becoming good stewards of nature is by living in nature, rather than trying to fix it with more innovation. I got a sense throughout this book that although he may sound impractical at times, there is great wisdom in his anti-modernity ideas.

I would be a huge hypocrite to say that I would want to live in the past that he is advocating. I was born and raised with the industrial and technological advancements of this futuristic world. I cannot imagine living without the conveniences and speed of the modern world. I’m curious though, whether his ideas changed or at least considered the practicalities and actual benefits of the current world. I think it is a valid question to ask considering that most, if not all of the essays in the book are published before I was even born. In the 19 years that has passed, considering he is still alive, maybe some of his ideas changed, or maybe evolved to consider the modern world.

Despite my defiance and inevitable acceptance of the modern world and its flaws, I still recognize the truth in his ideas, that the governments of the world failed to protect the environment, as they allowed corporations, entities demonstrably bigger than any single human or even small communities ever could, to destroy the environment. These corporations and even governments, after realizing what they did, just justified and tried to minimize them in the name of progress, and some don’t even stop. This realization should make us consider how we, as participants of the modern economy, became indirect participants of the destruction of our environment. They, and in turn we, failed the farmers, the local communities, and the environment in favor of the CEOs, conglomerates, and the economy.

The answer to the problem of the environment is not to stop these corporations and bring the present back to the way we used to in the past. It is merely wishful thinking to hope for such drastic undoing of what already is irreversible. The answer lies in all of us, in our daily responses or submission to society’s destructive ways. When we choose to recognize that there is indeed a problem, our response should be to change how we as individuals live in nature, before we advocate for big changes that we hope will solve all of our environmental problems. While big changes do change a lot, they also require changing immense things such as our faith in technologies, and our dependence on the economy to be good, which all requires the destruction of the environment one way or another.

Maybe the best course of action, after recognizing the problem, is for us as individuals to instill change within our ways first. We could vote with our money, and our faith. When we stop our faithful dependence, we rid ourselves of the obligation to participate in every destructive way that is destroying our environment. When we buy only from the corporations that do not actively destroy the environment, when we buy only what is necessary, we are still making some changes despite indirectly participating in the destructive economy. It is in these little ways that we can cultivate the necessary culture that cares for the environment.
entry.summary: I attempted to read this book two times before. I discovered it in a Jared Henderson book recommendation video on YouTube some year or two ago. The title hooked me so much that I romanticized reading it, and I even made my first blog referencing the title. But enough of my chatter, I have some words upon finishing this collection of essays by Wendell Berry. This book is long and dense, and requires more reading concentration to get something out of it, so here are some thoughts that remained from my reading.

entry.title: Some words about college
entry.content:
My first semester of college will officially end tomorrow, as I take my very last exams. Time flew by so fast that August 11, 2025, felt like half a year ago. I should have written here and there about my college experiences, but I never got around to writing consistently. I am sure I have some written fragments here and there, but I never sat down and wrote a complete essay, which I will do now.

Where should I start?

Maybe I’ll start with the first day of classes, which was August 11. I wore a green polo there. And as I entered the campus, I met A and we saw R. I said hi, and R’s friend, G, will become my very first friend. As I am waiting to enter my first class which is GMATH, I learned that G is also a CS student, and so we talked. I don’t even know how I socialized that well to get a friend already to be honest, and looking in hindsight, I really hit the jackpot. For our first class, we did an introduce yourself. We said our name, our past school, why we chose Computer Science and why chose Saint Louis University, and answered: What is the importance of GMATH? When it was my turn, I was nervous but I managed to introduce myself without shaming myself. I answered why SLU with “gusto ko magpakalayo,” my classmates laughed, but before I said that, my teacher also asked why did I not go to DMMMSU since there is a CS there. I later learned that he is a graduate of DMMMSU as well. In our second class, we met G. I remember us talking about computers and I was able to say that I use Linux, we did talk about Linux. The teacher never came to meet us but I have two friends now. Then, the same happened to our third class; we waited and talked. As we were waiting, we saw a boy standing alone on the bridge near the amphitheater. I think it was G who initiated a talk, so we are four now. We waited and talked until the class decided to leave. As we headed to leave the school, my newfound friends initiated a fist bump as a sign of goodbye, and that became a habit to us whenever we part our ways. We created a group chat that night, still named “K, G, G” on my side. I had three friends on the first day of school, which is a big accomplishment for me. Today, December 12, as I am writing this portion, we are still friends.

On the second day of classes, it was scheduled as our Orientation at the Main Campus, we had to go there before 7 AM. So, with my new friends, we went there. Only me, K, and G were together in the morning since G was late. But in the afternoon, I was with A. The whole experience was surreal to me. I did feel like I do not belong at times as I was surrounded by unfamiliar faces, but I did not allow that to undermine the positives. It is a privilege to study here in SLU, not because I think it is the best school, but because I am studying away from home, and for me that is the dream.

Before I even passed the SLU CEE, I already had a plan in my head that I would study either in UP, or UC for its trimester. I wanted to study in Baguio because I wanted to grow alone, to experience life without the constant watch of my parents. Since I was in elementary, I was used to having my Mama watch me since she is a teacher in my elementary school and I even had her as a teacher in 2nd and 4th grade. I was eventually given more freedom in high school since I now study at a different municipality, but at the end of the day, I was still going home. My desire to be alone and have more freedom is a dream to me, not as a sign of selfishness but as a desire to truly grow myself. I thought that going at home in college means I am still bound to the same habits and same environment. I thought that to truly become successful, I have to taste true freedom, which I have now. This plan of mine did not get cemented until I convinced my Mama. When I told her that I want to study in Baguio, she advised me to just study in DMMMSU, where I graduated senior high school. I remember saying to her that “I will not meet people… I will not grow when I have to go home everyday…”. I was anxious for about a month, as my future is still not according to my desires. Yet somehow, my Mama with the advice of my Titas as she said to me, decided that I will study in SLU, not in UC since my dream of studying in UP is not granted as I failed the UPCAT. I don’t actually have any plans before to study in SLU as I really wanted that UC trimester but my Mama did not want me to study in UC for some reason and in hindsight, I’m glad I went to SLU. I don’t know what my Tita A or Tita A told my Mama, but I’m glad she changed her mind.

I went from being anxious that I will have to settle for my old school to being excited for my future in SLU. Just to clarify, my reason for not wanting to go to DMMMSU is just the close distance to our home and the mere fact that I would have to go home everyday. I don’t think that SLU or any school in Baguio is superior. I just wanted some distance, and more freedom. I wanted to live alone. I know that it is a privilege. So I am committed to not waste this opportunity.

On the first week of classes from August 13 onward, I did feel a lot of things. First, I felt alien to this new environment. I had to live alone, which presents various challenges. I do not have the convenience of having my parents do things for me. So I had to do a lot of things myself. When I got to school, I would sometimes feel like I should not be here. But I was quick to adapt to a new routine, like walking for 15 minutes to my school and back to my dorm. I still feel jealous at times, but I am more than grateful for what I have now.

I also felt dumb, or to describe it better, I finally felt like I am not one of the smartest in the room. I was really humbled since from my elementary days until my senior high school, I felt like I was smart because I got good grades and even topped my class in my last year in senior high school. I know that I am bad at math, but my good grades kept me thinking that I am smart enough to be considered one. Upon meeting my classmates, I already saw some people who are way beyond me in terms of “smartness” and also practical abilities. They speak so fluently, they are so good at math, and they are also way advanced than me in programming and technological know-how. I finally met people I’ve been wanting to meet. Noticeably, I met someone who uses Linux as well and damn, he is way ahead of me. My friends alone are smarter than me in some ways. And I like it this way. I am finally a small fish surrounded by bigger fishes, which I know will motivate me to improve and grow bigger myself. Did this last paragraph make me sound like I’m big-headed? I hope not to sound that way. I am not bragging about myself being “smart”, I’m just saying that I considered myself smart since I’ve always had good grades. I am also not saying that I never met smarter people before, it’s just that I finally met the smart people in the niche things I am interested about, not just the smart who got good grades. But regardless, college indeed humbles you.

And most felt of all, I felt in control. I experienced being an adult at last. To me, this is the most beautiful part of going to college.

Aside from meeting friends and my classmates, I also met some of the best teachers I’ve ever met yet. Our major subject professors challenged us in ways that are not easy nor impossible. They were able to give us the best lectures, and I felt that every class was completely worth it. Some teachers also left more than knowledge to me personally, some of them became little inspirations, and some left impacting messages and lessons that I’ll definitely remember.

To Sir V: Thank you for the world-class lectures every single time you enter our class. I’ve always felt this immense sense of understanding every time you utter a word. Your occasional jokes are funny and relevant. Although your subject was the first time I got a line of 7, I still think that I learned so much in Discrete Mathematics and it was my fault for not taking math seriously in my formative years. That 99 prelim grade really made me think that I can take this easy, but what a turnaround. Your Christmas message to us really left something in me.

To Ma’am J: Thank you for the challenge. You made Introduction to Programming challenging, but as you said “it is not impossible”. I’ve enjoyed every lab activity, and I’ll remember my low scores in quizzes that pushed me to do better next time. When I saw how knowledgeable our programming professor is, that is you, I felt validated for choosing to study here.

To Ma’am B: Thank you for the motivation, thank you for always reminding us how we should take this first year as a practice for our higher years. Thank you for always relating our seemingly boring Introduction to Computing lessons to our future endeavors. I’ll remember the disciplinary lessons you have given us at times.

entry.title: Suffering and Morality
entry.content:
Suffering, the thought that there are people and animals experiencing pain and hardship, has been on my mind for weeks I suppose. It has been raining in that period of thinking, and I really had a lot of thoughts about the moral aspect of those suffering- specifically our moral obligation as individuals to help as much as we can, or at least start thinking about the suffering of others to hopefully inspire ourselves to make a contribution.

Earlier today, I watched Peter Singer’s talk at the Talks at Google YouTube Channel. I had nothing to do and my thoughts about suffering and morality just made me interested enough to watch it. Just a few weeks ago, around July, I read his famous essay talking about our moral obligation as individuals to alleviate suffering.

There are endless types of suffering, different people define and feel it differently. I’d like to define it myself, but I want to focus on human suffering for this brief essay. I do believe that certain animals do suffer, but I’d like to talk about it in a different essay. I define human suffering as:

  1. The lack of basic survival and safety needs which are food and water, shelter, medicine and healthcare.
  2. The lack of liberty and safety. Liberty is the situation where a person has the rights and protection not to be violated, under their country’s constitution and the accepted universal moral truths.
  3. The lack of emotional faculties such as a loving family and friends, and a good self identity.

In Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, my definition would cover the Physiological, Safety, and Love & Belonging levels. My definition of suffering is limited to the physical and emotional aspects of a person. I believe that a person who still lacks the types, categories, or criteria of suffering I made are in desperate need to be helped.

Just imagine the first one, despite the conveniences of the modern world, there are still people who only eat once a day or not at all, there are still people who live on the streets and beg, and there are still people who cannot access the medications and health services to ease their conditions and diseases. The suffering they are experiencing physically is unimaginable for most people. We feel everyday that our own “suffering” is the worst, yet there are people alive who are just alive because they are still somehow breathing. The concept of happiness is not even conceivable in my opinion when one does not have consistent access to the first set of needs. I don’t believe any optimist who would say that people can be happy when they cannot even survive like most pets. I acknowledge that there are people who are just lacking one or two of these needs at some times, and we might naturally consider them to suffer less, but the point still stands that these basic needs must be met all the time.

Next, the requirement of liberty and safety is another fundamental requirement to not suffer. Despite the world abandoning its barbaric practices in favor of more peaceful ones in general, there are still violations to peace happening all over the world. People suffer when they are used as slaves, detained, raped, abused, and more bad things done to them. These are what I consider liberty and safety violations, which require not a thing to be given, but for a thing not to be done. There are people out there that are living a good life and yet violated, and therefore, have suffered because of bad things done to them.

Lastly, there is the invisible suffering which resides in people’s brains. Our concept of suffering can also be felt even if we are in a safe place and with abundant basic needs. Mental health, or better called emotional health can be the greatest source of suffering to some. Psychologists cannot cure anyone of mental suffering, as they say. But why is that? It’s because we are complex, thinking beings. And it comes with it the toll on having the consciousness to suffer inside our heads. This type of suffering is the least understood one to this day, and some still think it is non existent. The emotional faculties I’m talking about are the people and ideas of ourselves which facilitates a better state of mind. I don’t want to talk about psychology since I don’t have a background on that, but I believe that one of the most important faculties is the presence of a loving family, which includes friends. The love which they bring to a person is so important to their self identity. ‘I am loved’, is perhaps the best way you can describe yourself.

I’d like to start this essay by talking about our role as individuals to be aware and take action amidst the many suffering in the world. Feeling sorry for people who suffer is the first step before we can take action. Just knowing and feeling empathetic is the first step to making a helpful contribution, even if it takes years before you take the first action.

For many people including me, the taking action part feels impossible or at least hard for the time being. Students like me, who have no jobs nor rich parents, cannot just go around helping people. We could volunteer, but we also have school and our own problems as growing adults which need our time. I’m not rationalizing myself to be moral despite not doing anything to help yet. I’m saying this because it is an important moral claim- that it is okay not to do anything yet, it is enough to simply be aware and be willing to help when opportunities come in the future.

One of the problems that arises when people read Singer’s essay is the implication that we ought to sacrifice every luxury to save people. Personally, I do believe in the essence of it, but what defines luxury? Is it morally bad to prioritize buying a big and beautiful house for your family instead of donating the money to charity? Singer’s concept of “equal moral worth” makes it hard to draw the line between what is enough for us and what ought to be given. But certainly, there are many luxuries people have such as having many mansions without people to live in them all, and having net worth in the millions and billions which are extreme cases of luxuries which can easily be said to be of lesser moral worth. I cannot draw the line for people, but personally, I have a line which I think makes sense to me, and people should have their own too.

Singer’s call to action- that we have a moral obligation to sacrifice luxuries to help people still holds. But there is a time when people cannot help, and it’s okay. It is a ‘blameless wrongdoing’ for people not to help, just because they still haven’t met the line of luxury, whatever that means to them.

So what should we do?

entry.title: The Places
entry.content:
I woke up one day after taking my afternoon nap. My lola told me to sleep in the afternoon for me to grow my height. Most of the time, I would just pretend to be sleeping but end up waking up a few hours later feeling like I was reborn. Most times, I slept on my lola and lolo’s house but there are times when my they would visit their riverside cabin made of bamboos. I took a swim on the river most days, I created sand balls and cured it under the sun, and I helped pick fishes that my lolo caught using a net. There is a steep road that led to the riverside and I would ride my toy car, sending me speeding downhill.

The river had a wide flat of sand, rocks, and an assortment of grasses. It was a river that traversed between the mountains and stretched for what felt like infinity. I only went to part of the river near my grandparent’s cabin. When I was six or seven, they built a small dam and an irrigation system which became another place for me to swim. On the dam, there is a 5 meter tower, which on top had the manual gears to control the dam’s flow. The dam had a wide slide that made the water flow through it with a speed that creates momentum when you slide on it and also creates a higher pressure stream of water which sends them rushing though a flat cemented region before falling on the untouched river. The dam attracted kids. There is a place for the normal kids where they can jump on a small elevated area and swim back and forth on the dam. But there is also a place for those kids who already had the nerves to take risks. There are deep parts of the dam which is too deep for even adults, but the most dangerous part of it was the shallow opening for the irrigation system. You can enter this opening, which is so dark and narrow from the outside. I never had the courage to even enter that opening, some kids did it as I fear if they would ever come back, and to make matters worse, that opening will never allow a person to get back from the other side. I’d like to imagine it as a death opening, wherein a sudden rise of the river or a thing entering it which blocks the way back will deliver someone inside to an untimely death. I never heard of someone getting killed by that opening, but who knows what sort of things already happened inside it. The opening allowed the water to flow from the dam to the narrow irrigation system which attracted mothers and kids. The girls would do their laundry their while the kids play along this narrow opening with a constant flow of water passing by.

My grandparents also had a mountain cabin, which is just a small resting place while my lolo cuts bamboos and my lola plants or harvests some edible plants. They sometimes take me hiking on this mountain. There is a cemented path where we walked, but it was mostly leaves and a lot of tree debris. There was nothing much to do on the mountains besides waiting for my grandparents to finish what they are doing, I would just eat a cracker and a soft drink while I wait for our eventual descent. Everyday was a fun day to go out and swim or hike, take a nap, and play the whole rest of the afternoon.

We live in my grandparents’ house. It is a two-story half cement, and half wooden house. Our room is in the ground floor, with my grandparents on the other room nearby. On the second floor are my titas. There is a wide space on the second floor where I would spend most of my time inside the house. There is a wooden staircase that led to a big door similar to the big church doors. It led to the front of the house and a view to the neighborhood. The walls is covered by picture frames and an altar lay at the center. I like to spend my time here reading or picture looking my books. I have a set of encyclopedias of different topics and random picture books. I would fall asleep here, and would wake up from either the call for lunch or the arrival of my mother. My mother worked in the outskirt of our town as a public school teacher. My father meanwhile worked somewhere far away.

On Sundays, we went to the town proper, which we call locally as “ili”, to go to the church and go to the public market (“palengke”) afterwards. This Sunday ritual made me love to go out in this little town because we always had burgers before going home. On special occasions, we went to Agoo, a nearby town more developed than ours. There is a Jollibee, malls, and a lot of toys. On rare occasions, we went to Baguio, the nearest city from our home. We would ride my lolo’s tricycle to go to the town proper, we would ride a jeep to go to Agoo, and we would ride a bus to go to Baguio City. My titas took me to some other places as well, they would bring me to their school and have me sleep on their apartments.

My senses travels in these few places near home. But my experiences revolves around the few frequent places I spent my days. My grandparents house, our neighborhood roads, and the river— these are my favorite places.

entry.title: Call me Ken.
entry.content: “Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can.” —Herman Melville
